content:
The image shows a corn ear with:
- Husks largely absent/stripped back, exposing the ear
- A prominent white-to-silvery gall at the top of the ear, beginning to turn dark (spore mass forming inside)
- The ear itself shows dark, black discoloration/spore masses mixed among the exposed kernels
- The overall structure is distorted with abnormal growths replacing normal ear development
- White/silvery tissue covering some areas transitioning to darker masses

This is a classic presentation of **Common Smut** (*Ustilago maydis*): white to silvery galls on the ear that later fill with dark (black/brown) spore masses. The large gall at the top with white covering turning to dark interior spores, combined with the black discoloration throughout the ear, matches the description precisely. Head Smut could be considered, but Head Smut produces teardrop-shaped ears lacking silks with stringy vascular bundles inside the spore mass, and typically replaces the entire ear/tassel. Here the galls are localized and the ear structure is partially intact, which is more characteristic of Common Smut.
